There was broad agreement that QPA calculation system readiness was around 65% (range 60–75%), with smaller plans facing data integration challenges. initial_posts.narrative: As an HHS regulatory attorney, I anticipate that in the first year of NSA implementation, activities will be substantial but uneven due to system readiness and data challenges. Approximately 8.5 million QPA calculations will be performed, as many plans struggle with insufficient data for uncommon services, leading to reliance on derived amounts or eligible databases. Over 15 million disclosure notices will be distributed, reflecting both plan EOB requirements and provider notice obligations to patients. Initial payments within the 30-day window will be made for about 6 million claims, as incomplete clean claims and system integration issues delay many payments. IDR cases initiated will number around 500,000, predominantly for emergency services (which cannot be waived) and non-emergency services at in-network facilities, with air ambulance representing a minor fraction. Uninsured and self-pay patients are handled under separate good faith estimate and patient-provider dispute resolution rules, not the standard IDR process, limiting their impact on these activities.

Uninsured and self-pay patients are protected through good faith estimate requirements and a separate patient-provider dispute resolution process, so they do not trigger NSA IDR or the notice-and-consent waiver provisions for insured individuals.

Network adequacy gradually improves as plans expand contracts to avoid IDR disputes, but consolidation among dominant hospital systems in rural regions holds the index to 0.70. Premiums rise about 2% as plans pass through higher allowed payment amounts from IDR outcomes and increased in-network cost-sharing subsidies. Overall, the policy achieves durable protection for most patients, but structural gaps in enforcement and network design prevent full elimination of surprise billing.

Second, the IDR process must be functioning as an effective backstop, with certified entities making timely and balanced decisions that do not systematically favor either side, thereby discouraging inflated offers and promoting in-network contracting. Third, enforcement must be robust: plans and providers must face credible penalties for noncompliance, and the Departments' complaint system must be accessible and responsive. Upstream, this requires that the notice and consent process not be abused to bypass protections, which relies on clear disclosure requirements and provider compliance. Without this, the predicted OON prevalence would likely be higher due to access issues.
